entries.6004b4590d6de8cc163ec9892339836dd3e5f968: <div sID="gen16786" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="55" osisID="Isa.55" sID="Isa.55"/> <div eID="gen16786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16787" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16788" type="x-p"/> As we had much of Christ in the <reference osisRef="Isa.53.1-Isa.53.12">53rd chapter</reference>, and much of the church of Christ in the <reference osisRef="Isa.54.1-Isa.54.17">54th chapter</reference>, so in this chapter we have much of the covenant of grace made with us in Christ. The "sure mercies of David," which are promised here (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.3">ver. 3</reference>), are applied by the apostle to the benefits which flow to us from the resurrection of Christ (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.34">Acts xiii. 34</reference>), which may serve as a key to this chapter; not but that it was intended for the comfort of the people of God that lived then, especially of the captives in Babylon, and others of the dispersed of Israel; but unto us was this gospel preached as well as unto them, and much more clearly and fully in the New Testament. Here is, I. A free and gracious invitation to all to come and take the benefit of gospel grace, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. Pressing arguments to enforce this invitation, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.2-Isa.55.4">ver. 2-4</reference>. III. A promise of the success of this invitation among the Gentiles, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.5">ver. 5</reference>. IV. An exhortation to repentance and reformation, with great encouragement given to hope for pardon thereupon, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.6-Isa.55.9">ver. 6-9</reference>. V. The ratification of all this, with the certain efficacy of the word of God, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.10-Isa.55.11">ver. 10, 11</reference>. And a particular instance of the accomplishment of it in the return of the Jews out of their captivity, which was intended for a sign of the accomplishment of all these other promises.
entries.44735471ac3361ad204a77a6d5c61e577022f75b: <div eID="gen16788" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16787" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Evangelical Invitations. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 706.)</title> <div sID="gen16789" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price. <hi type="super">2</hi> Wherefore do ye spend money for <hi type="italic">that which is</hi> not bread? and your labour for <hi type="italic">that which</hi> satisfieth not? hearken diligently unto me, and eat ye <hi type="italic">that which is</hi> good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness. <hi type="super">3</hi> Incline your ear, and come unto me: hear, and your soul shall live; and I will make an everlasting covenant with you, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the sure mercies of David. <hi type="super">4</hi> Behold, I have given him <hi type="italic">for</hi> a witness to the people, a leader and commander to the people. <hi type="super">5</hi> Behold, thou shalt call a nation <hi type="italic">that</hi> thou knowest not, and nations <hi type="italic">that</hi> knew not thee shall run unto thee because of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God, and for the Holy One of Israel; for he hath glorified thee. <div eID="gen16789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16790" type="x-p"/> Here, I. We are all invited to come and take the benefit of that provision which the grace of God has made for poor souls in the new covenant, of that which is the <hi type="italic">heritage of the servants of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.17">ch. liv. 17</reference>), and not only their heritage hereafter, but their cup now, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.1">v. 1</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen16790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16791" type="x-p"/> 1. Who are invited: <hi type="italic">Ho, every one.</hi> Not the Jews only, to whom first the word of salvation was sent, but the Gentiles, the poor and the maimed, the halt and the blind, are called to this marriage supper, whoever can be picked up out of the highways and the hedges. It intimates that in Christ there is enough for all and enough for each, that ministers are to make a general offer of life and salvation to all, that in gospel times the invitation should be more largely made than it had been and should be sent to the Gentiles, and that the gospel covenant excludes none that do not exclude themselves. The invitation is published with an <hi type="italic">Oyez-Ho,</hi> take notice of it. <hi type="italic">He that has ears to hear let him hear.</hi> <div eID="gen16791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16792" type="x-p"/> 2. What is the qualification required in those that shall be welcome—they must thirst. All shall be welcome to gospel grace upon those terms only that gospel grace be welcome to them. Those that are satisfied with the world and its enjoyments for a portion, and seek not for a happiness in the favour of God,—those that depend upon the merit of their own works for a righteousness, and see no need they have of Christ and his righteousness,—these do not thirst; they have no sense of their need, are in no pain or uneasiness about their souls, and therefore will not condescend so far as to be beholden to Christ. But those that thirst are invited to the waters, as those that labour, and are heavy-laden, are invited to Christ for rest. Note, Where God gives grace he first gives a thirsting after it; and, where he has given a thirsting after it, he will give it, <reference osisRef="Ps.81.10">Ps. lxxxi. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen16792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16793" type="x-p"/> 3. Whither they are invited: <hi type="italic">Come you to the waters.</hi> Come to the water-side, to the ports, and quays, and wharfs, on the navigable rivers, into which goods are imported; thither come and buy, for that is the market-place of foreign commodities; and to us they would have been for ever foreign if Christ had not brought in an everlasting righteousness. Come to Christ; for he is the fountain opened; he is the rock smitten. Come to holy ordinances, to those streams that make glad the city of our God; come to them, and though they may seem to you plain and common things, like waters, yet to those who believe in Christ the things signified will be as wine and mile, abundantly refreshing. Come to the healing waters; come to the living waters. Whoever will, let him come, and <hi type="italic">partake of the waters of life,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.22.17">Rev. xxii. 17</reference>. Our Saviour referred to it, <reference osisRef="John.7.37">John vii. 37</reference>. <hi type="italic">If any man thirst, let him come to me and drink.</hi> <div eID="gen16793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16794" type="x-p"/> 4. What they are invited to do. (1.) <hi type="italic">Come, and buy.</hi> Never did any tradesman court customers that he hoped to get by as Christ courts us to that which we only are to be gainers by. "Come and buy, and we can assure you you shall have a good bargain, which you will never repent of nor lose by. Come and buy; make it your own by an application of the grace of the gospel to yourselves; make it your own upon Christ's terms, nay, your own upon any terms, nor deliberating whether you shall agree to them." (2.) "<hi type="italic">Come, and eat;</hi> make it still more your own, as that which we eat is more our own than that which we only buy." We must buy the truth, not that we may lay it by to be looked at, but that we may feed and feast upon it, and that the spiritual life may be nourished and strengthened by it. We must buy necessary provisions for our souls, be willing to part with any thing, though ever so dear to us, so that we may but have Christ and his graces and comforts. We must part with sin, because it is an opposition to Christ, part with all opinion of our own righteousness, as standing in competition with Christ, and part with life itself, and its most necessary supports, rather than quit our interest in Christ. And, when we have bought what we need, let us not deny ourselves the comfortable use of it, but enjoy it, and eat the labour of our hands: <hi type="italic">Buy, and eat.</hi> <div eID="gen16794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16795" type="x-p"/> 5. What is the provision they are invited to: "<hi type="italic">Come, and buy wine and milk,</hi> which will not only quench the thirst" (fair water would do that), "but nourish the body, and revive the spirits." The world comes short of our expectations. We promise ourselves, at least, water in it, but we are disappointed of that, as <hi type="italic">the troops of Tema,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.6.19">Job vi. 19</reference>. But Christ outdoes our expectations. We come to the waters, and would be glad of them, but we find there wine and milk, which were the staple commodities of the tribe of Judah, and which the Shiloh of that tribe is furnished with to entertain the <hi type="italic">gathering of the people to him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Gen. xlix. 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.49.12">12</reference>. <hi type="italic">His eyes shall be red with wine and his teeth white with milk.</hi> We must come to Christ, to have milk for babes, to nourish and cherish those that are but lately born again; and with him strong men shall find that which will be a cordial to them: they shall have wine to make glad their hearts. We must part with our puddle-water, nay, with our poison, that we may procure this wine and milk. <div eID="gen16795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16796" type="x-p"/> 6. The free communication of this provision: <hi type="italic">Buy it without money, and without price.</hi> A strange way of buying, not only without ready money (that is common enough), but without any money, or the promise of any; yet it seems not so strange to those who have observed Christ's counsel to Laodicea, that was wretchedly poor, to <hi type="italic">come and buy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.3.17-Rev.3.18">Rev. iii. 17, 18</reference>. Our buying without money intimates, (1.) That the gifts offered us are invaluable and such as no price can be set upon. Wisdom is that which cannot be gotten for gold. (2.) That he who offers them has no need of us, nor of any returns we can make him. He makes us these proposals, not because he has occasion to sell, but because he has a disposition to give. (3.) That the things offered are already bought and paid for. Christ purchased them at the full value, with price, not with money, but with <hi type="italic">his own blood,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.19">1 Pet. i. 19</reference>. (4.) That we shall be welcome to the benefits of the promise, though we are utterly unworthy of them, and cannot make a tender of any thing that looks like a valuable consideration. We ourselves are not of any value, nor is any thing we have or can do, and we must own it, that, if Christ and heaven be ours, we may see ourselves for ever indebted to free grace. <div eID="gen16796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16797" type="x-p"/> II. We are earnestly pressed and persuaded (and O that we would be prevailed with!) to accept this invitation, and make this good bargain for ourselves. <div eID="gen16797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16798" type="x-p"/> 1. That which we are persuaded to is to hearken to God and to his proposals: "<hi type="italic">Hearken diligently unto me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.55.2">v. 2</reference>. Not only give me the hearing, but approve of what I say, and apply it to yourselves (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Incline your ear,</hi> as you do to that which you find yourselves concerned in and pleased with; bow the ear, and let the proud heart stoop to the humbling methods of the gospel; bend the ear this way, that you may hear with attention and remark; hear, <hi type="italic">and come unto me;</hi> not only come and treat with me, but comply with me, come up to my terms;" accept God's offers as very advantageous; answer his demands as very fit and reasonable. <div eID="gen16798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16799" type="x-p"/> 2. The arguments used to persuade us to this are taken, <div eID="gen16799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16800" type="x-p"/> (1.) From the unspeakable wrong we do to ourselves if we neglect and refuse this invitation: "<hi type="italic">Wherefore do you spend money for that which is not bread,</hi> which will not yield you, no, not beggar's food, dry bread, when with me you may have wine and milk without money? <hi type="italic">Wherefore do you spend your labour</hi> and toil <hi type="italic">for that which</hi> will not be so much as dry bread to you, for it <hi type="italic">satisfies not?</hi>" See here, [1.] The vanity of the things of this world. They are not bread, not proper food for a soul; they afford no suitable nourishment or refreshment. Bread is the staff of the natural life, but it affords no support at all to the spiritual life. All the wealth and pleasure in the world will not make one meal's meat for a soul. Eternal truth and eternal good are the only food for a rational and immortal soul, the life of which consists in reconciliation and conformity to God, and in union and communion with him, which the things of the world will not at all befriend. <hi type="italic">They satisfy not;</hi> they yield not any solid comfort and content to the soul, nor enable it to say, "Now I have what I would have." Nay, they do not satisfy even the appetites of the body. The more men have the more they would have, <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.8">Eccl. i. 8</reference>. Haman was unsatisfied in the midst of his abundance. They flatter, but they do not fill; they please for a while, like the dream of a hungry man, who awakes and his soul is empty. They soon surfeit, but they never satisfy; they cloy a man, but do not content him, or make him truly easy. It is all vanity and vexation. [2.] The folly of the children of this world. They spend their money and labour for these uncertain unsatisfying things. Rich people live by their money, poor people by their labour; but both mistake their truest interest, while the one is trading, the other toiling, for the world, both promising themselves satisfaction and happiness in it, but both miserably disappointed. God vouchsafes compassionately to reason with them: "Wherefore do you thus act against your own interest? Why do you suffer yourselves to be thus imposed upon?" Let us reason with ourselves, and let the result of these reasonings be a holy resolution not to <hi type="italic">labour for the meat that perishes, but for that which endures to everlasting life,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.6.27">John vi. 27</reference>. Let all the disappointments we meet with in the world help to drive us to Christ, and lead us to seek for satisfaction in him only. This is the way to make sure which will be made sure. <div eID="gen16800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16801" type="x-p"/> (2.) From the unspeakable kindness we do to ourselves if we accept this invitation and comply with it. [1.] hereby we secure to ourselves present pleasure and satisfaction: "If you hearken to Christ, you <hi type="italic">eat that which is good,</hi> which is both wholesome and pleasant, good in itself and good for you." God's good word and promise, a good conscience, and the comforts of God's good Spirit, are a continual feast to those that hearken diligently and obediently to Christ. Their souls shall <hi type="italic">delight themselves in fatness,</hi> that is, in the riches and most grateful delights. Here the invitation is not, "Come, and <hi type="italic">buy,</hi>" lest that should discourage, but, "Come, and <hi type="italic">eat;</hi> come and entertain yourselves with that which will be abundantly pleasing; eat, O friends!" It is sad to think that men should need to be courted thus to their own bliss. [2.] Hereby we secure to ourselves lasting happiness: "<hi type="italic">Hear, and your soul shall live;</hi> you shall not only be saved from perishing eternally, but you shall be eternally blessed:" for less than that cannot be the life of an immortal soul. The words of Christ are spirit and life, life to spirits (<reference osisRef="John.6.33">John vi. 33</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.6.63">63</reference>), the words of this life, <reference osisRef="Acts.5.20">Acts v. 20</reference>. On what easy terms is happiness offered to us! It is but "Hear, and you shall live." [3.] The great God graciously secures all this to us: "Come to me, <hi type="italic">and I will make an everlasting covenant with you,</hi> will put myself into covenant-relations and under covenant-engagements to you, and thereby settle upon you <hi type="italic">the sure mercies of David.</hi>" Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> If we come to God to serve him, he will covenant with us to do us good and make us happy; such are his condescension to us and concern for us. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> God's covenant with us is an everlasting covenant—its contrivance from everlasting, its continuance to everlasting. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> The benefits of this covenant are mercies suited to our case, who, being miserable, are the proper objects of mercy. They come from God's mercy, and are ordered every way in kindness to us. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> They are the mercies of David, such mercies as God promised to David (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.28-Ps.89.29">Ps. lxxxix. 28, 29</reference>, &c.), which are called <hi type="italic">the mercies of David his servant,</hi> and are appealed to by Solomon, <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.42">2 Chron. vi. 42</reference>. It shall be a covenant as sure as that with David, <reference osisRef="Jer.33.25-Jer.33.26">Jer. xxxiii. 25, 26</reference>. The covenant of royalty was a figure of the covenant of grace, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.5">2 Sam. xxiii. 5</reference>. Or, rather, by David here we are to understand the Messiah. Covenant-mercies are all <hi type="italic">his</hi> mercies; they are purchased by him; they are promised in him; they are treasured up in his hand, and out of his hand they are dispensed to us. He is the Mediator and trustee of the covenant; to him this is applied, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.34">Acts xiii. 34</reference>. They are the <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ta hosia</hi></hi> (the word used there, and by the Septuagint here)—<hi type="italic">the holy things</hi> of David, for they are confirmed by the holiness of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.35">Ps. lxxxix. 35</reference>) and are intended to advance holiness among men. <hi type="italic">Fifthly,</hi> They are sure mercies. The covenant, being well-ordered in all things, is sure. It is sure in the general proposal of it; God is real and sincere, serious and in earnest, in the offer of these mercies. It is sure in the particular application of it to believers; God's gifts and callings are without repentance. They are the mercies of David, and therefore sure, for in Christ the promises are all yea and amen. <div eID="gen16801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16802" type="x-p"/> III. Jesus Christ is promised for the making good of all the other promises which we are here invited to accept of, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.4">v. 4</reference>. He is that David whose sure mercies all the blessings and benefits of the covenant are. "And God has <hi type="italic">given him</hi> in his purpose and promise, has constituted and appointed him, and in the fulness of time will as surely send him as if he had already come, to be all that to us which is necessary to our having the benefit of these preparations." He has given him freely; for what more free than a gift? There was nothing in us to merit such a favour, but Christ is the gift of God. We want one, 1. To attest the truth of the promises which we are invited to take the benefit of; and Christ is given <hi type="italic">for a witness</hi> that God is willing to receive us into his favour upon gospel terms, to confirm the promises made unto the fathers, that we may venture our souls upon those promises with entire satisfaction. Christ is a faithful witness, we may take his word—a competent witness, for he lay in the bosom of the Father from eternity, and was perfectly apprised of the whole matter. Christ, as a prophet, testifies the will of God to the world; and to believe is to receive his testimony. 2. To assist us in closing with the invitation, and coming up to the terms of it. We know not how to find the way to the waters where we are to be supplied, but Christ is given to be <hi type="italic">a leader.</hi> We know not what to do that we may be qualified or it, and become sharers in it, but he is given for <hi type="italic">a commander,</hi> to show us what to do and enable us to do it. Much difficulty and opposition lie in our way to Christ; we have spiritual enemies to grapple with, but, to animate us for the conflict, we have a good captain, like Joshua, a leader and commander to tread our enemies under our feet and to put us in possession of the land of promise. Christ is a commander by his precept and a leader by his example; our business is to obey him and follow him. <div eID="gen16802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16803" type="x-p"/> IV. The Master of the feast being fixed, it is next to be furnished with guests, for the provision shall not be lost, nor made in vain, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.5">v. 5</reference>. 1. The Gentiles shall be called to this feast, shall be invited out of the highways and the hedges: "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt call a nation that thou knowest not,</hi> that is, that was not formerly called and owned as thy nation, that thou didst not send prophets to as to Israel, the people whom God knew above all the families of the earth." The Gentiles shall now be favoured as they never were before; their knowing God is said to be rather their <hi type="italic">being known of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.4.9">Gal. iv. 9</reference>. 2. They shall come at the call: <hi type="italic">Nations that knew not thee shall run unto thee;</hi> those that had long been afar off from Christ shall be made nigh; those that had been running from him shall run to him, with the greatest speed and alacrity imaginable. There shall be a concourse of believing Gentiles to Christ, who, being lifted up from the earth, will draw all men to him. Now see the reason, (1.) Why the Gentiles will thus flock to Christ; it is <hi type="italic">because of the Lord his God,</hi> because he is the Son of God, and is declared to be so with power, because they now see his God is one with whom they have to do, and there is no coming to him as their God but by making an interest in his Son. Those that are brought to be acquainted with God, and understand how the concern lies between them and him, cannot but run to Jesus Christ, who is the only Mediator between God and Man, and there is no coming to God but by him. (2.) Why God will bring them to him; it is because he is the Holy One of Israel, true to his promises, and he has promised to glorify him by giving him the heathen for his inheritance. When Greeks began to enquire after Christ he said, <hi type="italic">The hour has come that the Son of man should be glorified,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.12.22-John.12.23">John xii. 22, 23</reference>. And his being glorified in his resurrection and ascension was the great argument by which multitudes were wrought upon to run to him.
entries.39bac09c34ee1292630ad76599088e16b3e5fd2b: <div eID="gen16803" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Evangelical Invitations. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 706.)</title> <div sID="gen16804" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Seek ye the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> while he may be found, call ye upon him while he is near: <hi type="super">7</hi> Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts: and let him return unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon. <hi type="super">8</hi> For my thoughts <hi type="italic">are</hi> not your thoughts, neither <hi type="italic">are</hi> your ways my ways, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">9</hi> For <hi type="italic">as</hi> the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts. <hi type="super">10</hi> For as the rain cometh down, and the snow from heaven, and returneth not thither, but watereth the earth, and maketh it bring forth and bud, that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater: <hi type="super">11</hi> So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper <hi type="italic">in the thing</hi> whereto I sent it. <hi type="super">12</hi> For ye shall go out with joy, and be led forth with peace: the mountains and the hills shall break forth before you into singing, and all the trees of the field shall clap <hi type="italic">their</hi> hands. <hi type="super">13</hi> Instead of the thorn shall come up the fir tree, and instead of the brier shall come up the myrtle tree: and it shall be to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> for a name, for an everlasting sign <hi type="italic">that</hi> shall not be cut off. <div eID="gen16804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16805" type="x-p"/> We have here a further account of that covenant of grace which is made with us in Jesus Christ, both what is required and what is promised in the covenant, and of those considerations that are sufficient abundantly to confirm our believing compliance with and reliance on that covenant. This gracious discovery of God's good-will to the children of men is not to be confined either to the Jew or to the Gentile, to the Old Testament or to the New, much less to the captives in Babylon. No, both the precepts and the promises are here given to all, to <hi type="italic">every one that thirsts after happiness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.55.1">v. 1</reference>. And who does not? Hear this, and live. <div eID="gen16805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16806" type="x-p"/> I. Here is a gracious offer made of pardon, and peace, and all happiness, to poor sinners, upon gospel terms, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.6-Isa.55.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. <div eID="gen16806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16807" type="x-p"/> 1. Let them pray, and their prayers shall be heard and answered (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Seek the Lord while he may be found.</hi> Seek him whom you have left by revolting from your allegiance to him and whom you have lost by provoking him to withdraw his favour from you. <hi type="italic">Call upon him</hi> now <hi type="italic">while he is near,</hi> and within call." Observe here, <div eID="gen16807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16808" type="x-p"/> (1.) The duties required. [1.] "Seek the Lord. Seek to him, and enquire of him, as your oracle. <hi type="italic">Ask the law at his mouth. What wilt thou have me to do?</hi> Seek for him, and enquire after him, as your portion and happiness; seek to be reconciled to him and acquainted with him, and to be happy in his favour. Be sorry that you have lost him; be solicitous to find him; take the appointed method of finding him, making use of Christ as your way, the Spirit as your guide, and the word as your rule." [2.] "Call upon him. Pray to him, to be reconciled, and, being reconciled, pray to him for every thing else you have need of." <div eID="gen16808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16809" type="x-p"/> (2.) The motives made use of to press these duties upon us: <hi type="italic">While he may be found—while he is near.</hi> [1.] It is implied that now God is near and will be found, so that it shall not be in vain to seek him and to call upon him. Now his patience is waiting on us, his word is calling to us, and his Spirit striving with us. Let us now improve our advantages and opportunities; for now is the accepted time. But, [2.] There is a day coming when he will be afar off, and will not be found, when the day of his patience is over, and his Spirit will strive no more. There may come such a time in this life, when the heart is incurably hardened; it is certain that at death and judgment the door will be <hi type="italic">shut,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.16.26">Luke xvi. 26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.13.25-Luke.13.26">xiii. 25, 26</reference>. Mercy is now offered, but then judgment without mercy will take place. <div eID="gen16809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16810" type="x-p"/> 2. Let them repent and reform, and their sins shall be pardoned, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.7">v. 7</reference>. Here is a call to the unconverted, to <hi type="italic">the wicked and the unrighteous</hi>—to the wicked, who live in known gross sins, to the unrighteous, who live in the neglect of plain duties: to them is the word of this salvation sent, and all possible assurance given that penitent sinners shall find God a pardoning God. Observe here, <div eID="gen16810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16811" type="x-p"/> (1.) What it is to repent. There are two things involved in repentance:—[1.] It is to turn from sin; it is to forsake it. It is to leave it, and to leave it with loathing and abhorrence, never to return to it again. The wicked must <hi type="italic">forsake his way,</hi> his evil way, as we would forsake a false way that will never bring us to the happiness we aim at, and a dangerous way, that leads to destruction. Let him not take one step more in that way. Nay, there must be not only a change of the way, but a change of the mind; the unrighteous must <hi type="italic">forsake his thoughts.</hi> Repentance, if it be true, strikes at the root, and washes the heart from wickedness. We must alter our judgments concerning persons and things, dislodge the corrupt imaginations and quit the vain pretences under which an unsanctified heart shelters itself. Note, It is not enough to break off from evil practices, but we must enter a caveat against evil thoughts. Yet this is not all: [2.] To repent is to <hi type="italic">return to the Lord;</hi> to return to him as our God, our sovereign Lord, against whom we have rebelled, and to whom we are concerned to reconcile ourselves; it is to return to the Lord as the fountain of life and living waters, which we had forsaken for broken cisterns. <div eID="gen16811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16812" type="x-p"/> (2.) What encouragement we have thus to repent. If we do so, [1.] God <hi type="italic">will have mercy.</hi> He will not deal with us as our sins have deserved, but will have compassion on us. Misery is the object of mercy. Now both the consequences of sin, by which we have become truly miserable (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.5-Ezek.16.6">Ezek. xvi. 5, 6</reference>), and the nature of repentance, by which we are made sensible of our misery and are brought to bemoan ourselves (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.18">Jer. xxxi. 18</reference>), both these make us objects of pity, and with God there are tender mercies. [2.] <hi type="italic">He will abundantly pardon. He will multiply to pardon</hi> (so the word is), as we have multiplied to offend. Though our sins have been very great and very many, and though we have often backslidden and are still prone to offend, yet God will repeat his pardon, and welcome even backsliding children that return to him in sincerity. <div eID="gen16812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16813" type="x-p"/> II. Here are encouragements given us to accept this offer and to venture our souls upon it. For, look which way we will, we find enough to confirm us in our belief of its validity and value. <div eID="gen16813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16814" type="x-p"/> 1. If we look up to heaven, we find God's counsels there high and transcendent, his thoughts and ways infinitely above ours, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.8-Isa.55.9">v. 8, 9</reference>. The wicked are urged to forsake their evil ways and thoughts (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.7">v. 7</reference>) and to return to God, that is, to bring their ways and thoughts to concur and comply with his; "for" (says he) "my thoughts and ways are not as yours. Yours are conversant only about things beneath; they are of the earth earthy: but mine are above, <hi type="italic">as the heaven is high above the earth;</hi> and, if you would approve yourselves true penitents, yours must be so too, and your affections must be set on things above." Or, rather, it is to be understood as an encouragement to us to depend upon God's promise to pardon sin, upon repentance. Sinners may be ready to fear that God will not be reconciled to them, because they could not find in their hearts to be reconciled to one who should have so basely and so frequently offended them. "But" (says God) "my thoughts in this matter are not as yours, but as far above them as the heaven is above the earth." They are so in other things. Men's sentiments concerning sin, and Christ, and holiness, concerning this world and the other, are vastly different from God's; but in nothing more than in the matter of reconciliation. We think God apt to take offence and backward to forgive—that, if he forgives once, he will not forgive a second time. Peter thought it a great deal to <hi type="italic">forgive seven times</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.18.21">Matt. xviii. 21</reference>), and a hundred pence go far with us; but God meets returning sinners with pardoning mercy; he forgives freely, and as he gives: it is without upbraiding. We forgive and cannot forget; but, when God forgives sin, he remembers it no more. Thus God invites sinners to return to him, by possessing them with good thoughts of him, as <reference osisRef="Jer.31.20">Jer. xxxi. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen16814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16815" type="x-p"/> 2. If we look down to this earth, we find God's word there powerful and effectual, and answering all its great intentions, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.10-Isa.55.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. Observe here, (1.) The efficacy of God's word in the kingdom of nature. He saith to the snow, Be thou on the earth; he appoints when it shall come, to what degree, and how long it shall lie there; he saith so <hi type="italic">to the small rain and the great rain of his strength,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.37.6">Job xxxvii. 6</reference>. And according to his order they come down from heaven, and do <hi type="italic">whatsoever he commands them upon the face of the world, whether it be for correction, or for his land, or for mercy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.55.12-Isa.55.13">v. 12, 13</reference>. It returns not <hi type="italic">re infectâ—without having accomplished its end,</hi> but waters the earth, which he is therefore said to do <hi type="italic">from his chambers,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.104.13">Ps. civ. 13</reference>. And the watering of the earth is in order to its fruitfulness. Thus he makes it to <hi type="italic">bring forth and bud,</hi> for the products of the earth depend upon the dews of heaven; and thus it gives not only <hi type="italic">bread to the eater,</hi> present maintenance to the owner and his family, but <hi type="italic">seed</hi> likewise <hi type="italic">to the sower,</hi> that he may have food for another year. The husbandman must be a sower as well as an eater, else he will soon see the end of what he has. (2.) The efficacy of his word in the kingdom of providence and grace, which is as certain as the former: "<hi type="italic">So shall my word be,</hi> as powerful in the mouth of prophets as it is in the hand of providence; <hi type="italic">it shall not return unto me void,</hi> as unable to effect what it was sent for, or meeting with an insuperable opposition; no, <hi type="italic">it shall accomplish that which I please</hi>" (for it is the declaration of his will, according to the counsel of which he works all things) "<hi type="italic">and it shall prosper in the thing for which I sent it.</hi>" This assures us, [1.] That the promises of God shall all have their full accomplishment in due time, and not one iota or tittle of them shall fail, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.56">1 Kings viii. 56</reference>. These promises of mercy and grace shall have as real an effect upon the souls of believers, for their sanctification and comfort, as ever the rain had upon the earth, to make it fruitful. [2.] That according to the different errands on which the word is sent it will have its different effects. If it be not a savour of life unto life, it will be a savour of death unto death; if it do not convince the conscience and soften the heart, it will sear the conscience and harden the heart; if it do not ripen for heaven, it will ripen for hell. See <reference osisRef="Isa.6.9">ch. vi. 9</reference>. One way or other, it will take effect. [3.] That Christ's coming into the world, as the dew from heaven (<reference osisRef="Hos.14.5">Hos. xiv. 5</reference>), will not be in vain. For, if Israel be not gathered, he will be glorious in the conversion of the Gentiles; to them therefore the tenders of grace must be made when the Jews refuse them, that the wedding may be furnished with guests and the gospel not return void. <div eID="gen16815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16816" type="x-p"/> 3. If we take a special view of the church, we shall find what great things God has done, and will do, for it (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.12-Isa.55.13">v. 12, 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">You shall go out with joy, and be led forth with peace.</hi> This refers, (1.) To the deliverance and return of the Jews out of Babylon. They shall go out of their captivity, and be led forth towards their own land again. God will go before them as surely, though not as sensibly, as before their fathers in the pillar of cloud and fire. They shall go out, not with trembling, but with triumph, not with any regret to part with Babylon, or any fear of being fetched back, but <hi type="italic">with joy</hi> and <hi type="italic">peace.</hi> Their journey home over the mountains shall be pleasant, and they shall have the good-will and good wishes of all the countries they pass through. <hi type="italic">The hills</hi> and their inhabitants <hi type="italic">shall,</hi> as in a transport of joy, <hi type="italic">break forth into singing;</hi> and, if the people should altogether hold their peace, even <hi type="italic">the trees of the field</hi> would attend them with their applauses and acclamations. And, when they come to their own land, it shall be ready to bid them welcome; for, whereas they expected to find it all overgrown with briers and thorns, it shall be set with <hi type="italic">fir-trees and myrtle-trees:</hi> for, though it lay desolate, yet it <hi type="italic">enjoyed its sabbaths</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.34">Lev. xxvi. 34</reference>), which, when they were over, like the land after the sabbatical year, it was the better for. And this shall redound much to the honour of God and be to him <hi type="italic">for a name.</hi> But, (2.) Without doubt it looks further. This shall be <hi type="italic">for an everlasting sign,</hi> that it, [1.] The redemption of the Jews out of Babylon shall be a ratification of those promises that relate to gospel times. The accomplishment of the predictions relating to that great deliverance would be a pledge and earnest of the performance of all the other promises; for thereby it shall appear that <hi type="italic">he is faithful who has promised.</hi> [2.] It shall be a representation of the blessings promised and a type and figure of them. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Gospel grace will set those at liberty that were in bondage to sin and Satan. They <hi type="italic">shall go out and be led forth.</hi> Christ shall make them free, and then they shall be free indeed. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It will fill those with joy that were melancholy. <reference osisRef="Ps.14.7">Ps. xiv. 7</reference>, <hi type="italic">Jacob shall rejoice, and Israel shall be glad.</hi> The earth and the inferior part of the creation shall share in the joy of this salvation, <reference osisRef="Ps.94.11-Ps.94.12">Ps. xciv. 11, 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> It will make a great change in men's characters. Those that were as thorns and briers, good for nothing but the fire, nay, hurtful and vexatious, shall become graceful and useful as the fir-tree and the myrtle-tree. Thorns and briers came in with sin and were the fruits of the curse, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.18">Gen. iii. 18</reference>. The raising of pleasant trees in the room of them signifies the removal of the curse of the law and the introduction of gospel blessings. The church's enemies were as thorns and briers; but, instead of them, God will raise up friends to be her protection and ornament. Or it may denote the world's growing better; instead of a generation of thorns and briers, there shall come up a generation of fir-trees and myrtles; the children shall be wiser and better than the parents. And, <hi type="italic">fourthly,</hi> in all this God shall be glorified. It shall be to him for a name, by which he will be made known and praised, and by it the people of God shall be encouraged. It shall be for an everlasting sign of God's favour to them, assuring them that, though it may for a time be clouded, it shall never <hi type="italic">be cut off.</hi> The covenant of grace is an everlasting covenant; for the present blessings of it are signs of everlasting ones.  <chapter eID="Isa.55"/> <div eID="gen16816" type="x-p"/>

entries.2ae51847cae3af11a5b11634161d9ae8c4411b02: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9367"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 55</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.55.1-Isa.55.13">Is 55:1-13</reference>. The Call of the Gentile World to Faith the Result of God's Grace to the Jews First.</title> <div sID="gen16165" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9367"/><hi type="bold">1. every one--</hi>After the special privileges of Israel (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.1-Isa.54.17">Is 54:1-17</reference>) there follow, as the consequence, the universal invitation to the Gentiles (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.47">Lu 24:47</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.12">Ro 11:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.15">15</reference>).<div eID="gen16165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16166" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ho--</hi>calls the most earnest attention.<div eID="gen16166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16167" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thirsteth--</hi>has a keen sense of need (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.6">Mt 5:6</reference>).<div eID="gen16167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16168" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">waters ... wine and milk--</hi>a gradation. Not merely water, which is needed to maintain life at all, but wine and milk to strengthen, cheer, and nourish; the spiritual blessings of the Gospel are meant (<reference osisRef="Isa.25.6">Is 25:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Song.5.1">So 5:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.7.37">Joh 7:37</reference>). "Waters," plural, to denote abundance (<reference osisRef="Isa.43.20">Is 43:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.3">44:3</reference>).<div eID="gen16168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16169" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no money--</hi>Yet, in <reference osisRef="Isa.55.2">Is 55:2</reference>, it is said, "ye spend money." A seeming paradox. Ye are really spiritual bankrupts: but thinking yourselves to have money, namely, a devotion of your own making, ye lavish it on that "which is not bread," that is, on idols, whether literal or spiritual.<div eID="gen16169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16170" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">buy ... without money--</hi>another paradox. We are bought, but not with a price paid by ourselves (<reference osisRef="1Cor.6.20">1Co 6:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.18">1Pe 1:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.19">19</reference>). In a different sense we are to "buy" salvation, namely, by parting with everything which comes between us and Christ who has bought it for us and by making it our own (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.44">Mt 13:44</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.46">46</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.12.33">Lu 12:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.3.18">Re 3:18</reference>). <div eID="gen16170" type="x-p"/>
entries.5838e38a01591bff04162e8a4b24a9f5392f40a9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9368"/><div sID="gen16171" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9368"/><hi type="bold">2. not bread--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Hab.2.13">Ha 2:13</reference>). "Bread of deceit" (<reference osisRef="Prov.20.17">Pr 20:17</reference>). Contrast this with the "bread of life" (<reference osisRef="John.6.32">Joh 6:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.6.35">35</reference>; also <reference osisRef="Luke.14.16-Luke.14.20">Lu 14:16-20</reference>).<div eID="gen16171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16172" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">satisfieth not--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.8">Ec 1:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.8">4:8</reference>).<div eID="gen16172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16173" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hearken ... and eat--</hi>When two imperatives are joined, the second expresses the consequence of obeying the command in the first (<reference osisRef="Gen.42.18">Ge 42:18</reference>). By hearkening ye shall eat. So in <reference osisRef="Isa.55.1">Is 55:1</reference>, "buy and eat." By buying, and so making it your own, ye shall eat, that is, experimentally enjoy it (<reference osisRef="John.6.53">Joh 6:53</reference>). Compare the invitation (<reference osisRef="Prov.9.5">Pr 9:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.9.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.22.4">Mt 22:4</reference>).<div eID="gen16173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16174" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fatness--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.36.8">Psa 36:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.63.5">63:5</reference>). <div eID="gen16174" type="x-p"/>
entries.830954b731b833f9217ebd04c951b90516110531: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9369"/><div sID="gen16175" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9369"/><hi type="bold">3. me ... live--</hi>by coming to me ye shall live: for "I am the life" (<reference osisRef="John.14.6">Joh 14:6</reference>).<div eID="gen16175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16176" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">everlasting covenant--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.32.40">Jr 32:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.5">2Sa 23:5</reference>).<div eID="gen16176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16177" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with you ... David--</hi>God's covenant is with the antitypical David, Messiah (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.23">Eze 34:23</reference>), and so with us by our identification with Him.<div eID="gen16177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16178" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sure--</hi>answering to "everlasting," irrevocable, unfailing, to be relied on (Psa 89:2-4, 28, 29, 34-36; <reference osisRef="Jer.33.20">Jr 33:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.33.21">21</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.15">2Sa 7:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.18-2Cor.1.20">2Co 1:18-20</reference>).<div eID="gen16178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16179" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mercies of David--</hi>the mercies of grace (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.7">Is 63:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.1.16">Joh 1:16</reference>) which I covenanted to give to David, and especially to Messiah, his antitype. Quoted in <reference osisRef="Acts.13.34">Ac 13:34</reference>. <div eID="gen16179" type="x-p"/>
entries.1aedb2cffd0135d73f63716635263118bddf5eb8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9370"/><div sID="gen16180" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9370"/><hi type="bold">4. him--</hi>the mystical David (<reference osisRef="Ezek.37.24">Eze 37:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.25">25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.30.9">Jr 30:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.3.5">Ho 3:5</reference>). Given by God (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.6">Is 49:6</reference>).<div eID="gen16180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16181" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">witness--</hi>He bore witness even unto death for God, to His law, claims, and plan of redeeming love (<reference osisRef="John.18.37">Joh 18:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.5">Re 1:5</reference>). Revelation is a "testimony"; because it is propounded to be received on the authority of the Giver, and not merely because it can be proved by arguments.<div eID="gen16181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16182" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">commander--</hi>"preceptor" [Horsley]; "lawgiver" [Barnes].<div eID="gen16182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16183" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to the people--</hi>rather, "peoples." <div eID="gen16183" type="x-p"/>
entries.ac77918e16ba83df9ac6ddec110de072fb41b285: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9371"/><div sID="gen16184" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9371"/><hi type="bold">5. thou--</hi>Jehovah addresses Messiah.<div eID="gen16184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16185" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">call ... run--</hi>God must call, before man can, or will, run (<reference osisRef="Song.1.4">So 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.6.44">Joh 6:44</reference>). Not merely come, but run eagerly.<div eID="gen16185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16186" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou knowest not--</hi>now as thy people (so in <reference osisRef="Matt.7.23">Mt 7:23</reference>).<div eID="gen16186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16187" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nation ... nations--</hi>gradation; from Israel, one nation, the Gospel spread to many nations, and will do so more fully on Israel's conversion.<div eID="gen16187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16188" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">knew not thee--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.52.15">Is 52:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.11">Ep 2:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.12">12</reference>).<div eID="gen16188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16189" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because of ... thy God ... glorified thee--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.60.5">Is 60:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.60.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.8.23">Zec 8:23</reference>); where similar language is directed to Israel, because of the identification of Israel with Messiah, who is the ideal Israel (<reference osisRef="Matt.2.15">Mt 2:15</reference>; compare with <reference osisRef="Hos.11.1">Ho 11:1</reference>; see <reference osisRef="Acts.3.13">Ac 3:13</reference>). <div eID="gen16189" type="x-p"/>
entries.67d025b295bc1a9ab9df56ce2acd263029151625: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9372"/><div sID="gen16190" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9372"/>6. The condition and limit in the obtaining of the spiritual benefits (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.1-Isa.3.1">Is 55:1-3): (1</reference>) Seek the Lord. (2) Seek Him while He is to be found (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.1">Is 65:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.32.6">Psa 32:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.25.1-Matt.25.13">Mt 25:1-13</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.7.34">Joh 7:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.8.21">8:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.2">2Co 6:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.2.3">He 2:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.13">3:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.15">15</reference>).<div eID="gen16190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16191" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">call--</hi>casting yourselves wholly on His mercy (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.13">Ro 10:13</reference>). Stronger than "seek"; so "near" is more positive than "while He may be found" (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.8">Ro 10:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.9">9</reference>).<div eID="gen16191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16192" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">near--</hi>propitious (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.18">Psa 34:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.145.18">145:18</reference>). <div eID="gen16192" type="x-p"/>
entries.b5d3d39256b003d5fac59f32795af303c36d23da: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9373"/><div sID="gen16193" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9373"/><hi type="bold">7. unrighteous--</hi>Hebrew, "man of iniquity"; true of all men. The "wicked" sins more openly in "his way"; the "unrighteous" refers to the more subtle workings of sin in the "thoughts." All are guilty in the latter respect, thought many fancy themselves safe, because not openly "wicked in ways" (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.11">Psa 94:11</reference>). The parallelism is that of gradation. The progress of the penitent is to be from negative reformation, "forsaking his way," and a farther step, "his thoughts," to positive repentance, "returning to the Lord" (the only true repentance, <reference osisRef="Zech.12.10">Zec 12:10</reference>), and making God his God, along with the other children of God (the crowning point; appropriation of God to ourselves: "to our God"). "Return" implies that man originally walked with God, but has apostatized. Isaiah saith, "our God," the God of the believing Israelites; those themselves redeemed desire others to come to their God (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.8">Psa 34:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.22.17">Re 22:17</reference>).<div eID="gen16193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16194" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">abundantly pardon--</hi>Literally, "multiply to pardon," still more than "have mercy"; God's graciousness is felt more and more the longer one knows Him (<reference osisRef="Ps.130.7">Psa 130:7</reference>). <div eID="gen16194" type="x-p"/>
entries.e147f0ba2014b21d0c61dd5896611e953362af01: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9374"/><div sID="gen16195" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9374"/><hi type="bold">8. For--</hi>referring to <reference osisRef="Isa.55.7">Is 55:7</reference>. You need not doubt His willingness "abundantly to pardon" (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.55.12">Is 55:12</reference>); for, though "the wicked" man's "ways," and "the unrighteous man's thoughts," are so aggravated as to seem unpardonable, God's "thoughts" and "ways" in pardoning are not regulated by the proportion of the former, as man's would be towards his fellow man who offended him; compare the "for" (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.11">Psa 25:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.5.19">Ro 5:19</reference>). <div eID="gen16195" type="x-p"/>
entries.170aa832589efa01a9ae081e973277d2f62e3188: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9375"/><div sID="gen16196" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9375"/>9. (<reference osisRef="Ps.57.10">Psa 57:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.89.2">89:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.103.11">103:11</reference>). "For" is repeated from <reference osisRef="Isa.55.8">Is 55:8</reference>. But Maurer, after the negation, translates, "but." <div eID="gen16196" type="x-p"/>
entries.3eedd88a4789aa393b659fbf68d1388c260854b6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9376"/><div sID="gen16197" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9376"/>10. The hearts of men, once barren of spirituality, shall be made, by the outpouring of the Spirit under Messiah, to bear fruits of righteousness (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.6">Is 5:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.2">De 32:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.4">2Sa 23:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.72.6">Psa 72:6</reference>).<div eID="gen16197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16198" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">snow--</hi>which covers plants from frost in winter; and, when melted in spring, waters the earth.<div eID="gen16198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16199" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">returneth not--</hi>void; as in <reference osisRef="Isa.55.11">Is 55:11</reference>; it returns not in the same shape, or without "accomplishing" the desired end.<div eID="gen16199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16200" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bud--</hi>germinate. <div eID="gen16200" type="x-p"/>
entries.0fa21115ec5dc95b5dfe77c0b8d5681751bcc064: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9377"/><div sID="gen16201" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9377"/>11. (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.35">Mt 24:35</reference>). Rain may to us seem lost when it falls on a desert, but it fulfils some purpose of God. So the gospel word falling on the hard heart; it sometimes works a change at last; and even if so, it leaves men without excuse. The full accomplishment of this verse, and <reference osisRef="Isa.55.12">Is 55:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.13">13</reference>, is, however, to be at the Jews' final restoration and conversion of the world (Is 11:9-12; 60:1-5, 21). <div eID="gen16201" type="x-p"/>
entries.7b7d8d40cab4c998eeb245f3c02f3fa821fdf691: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9378"/><div sID="gen16202" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9378"/><hi type="bold">12. go out--</hi>from the various countries in which ye (the Jews) are scattered, to your own land (<reference osisRef="Ezek.11.17">Eze 11:17</reference>).<div eID="gen16202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16203" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">led--</hi>by Messiah, your "Leader" (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.4">Is 55:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.52.12">Is 52:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.2.12">Mi 2:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.13">13</reference>).<div eID="gen16203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16204" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mountains ... trees, &c.--</hi>images justly used to express the seeming sympathy of nature with the joy of God's people. For, when sin is removed, the natural world shall be delivered from "vanity," and be renewed, so as to be in unison with the regenerated moral world (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.23">Is 44:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.98.8">Psa 98:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.19-Rom.8.22">Ro 8:19-22</reference>). <div eID="gen16204" type="x-p"/>
entries.c388a54019dca149c3e16627d99df6264619762c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9379"/><div sID="gen16205" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9379"/><hi type="bold">13. thorn--</hi>emblem of the wicked (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.6">2Sa 23:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.7.4">Mi 7:4</reference>).<div eID="gen16205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16206" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fir tree--</hi>the godly (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.13">Is 60:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.92.12">Psa 92:12</reference>). Compare as to the change wrought, <reference osisRef="Rom.6.19">Ro 6:19</reference>.<div eID="gen16206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16207" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brier--</hi>emblem of uncultivation (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.6">Is 5:6</reference>).<div eID="gen16207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16208" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">myrtle--</hi>Hebrew, Hedes, from which comes Hedassah, the original name of Esther. Type of the Christian Church; for it is a lowly, though beautiful, fragrant, and evergreen shrub (<reference osisRef="Ps.92.13">Psa 92:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.92.14">14</reference>).<div eID="gen16208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16209" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for a name ... everlasting sign--</hi>a perpetual memorial to the glory of Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Jer.13.11">Jr 13:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.33.9">33:9</reference>). <chapter eID="Isa.55"/>

entries.853512ed10f0752b85685bda670071c6a78a8dc7: <div eID="gen28697" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen28698" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen28699" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28699" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28698" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen28700" type="x-p"/> This chapter first displays the fullness, freeness, excellence, and everlasting nature of the blessings of the Gospel, and foretells again the enlargement of Messiah's kingdom, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.1-Isa.55.5">Isa 55:1-5</reference>. This view leads the prophet to exhort all to seize the precious opportunity of sharing in such blessings, which were not, however, to be expected without repentance and reformation, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.6">Isa 55:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.7">Isa 55:7</reference>. And as the things now and formerly predicted were so great as to appear incredible, the prophet points to the omnipotence of God, who would infallibly accomplish his word, and bring about those glorious deliverances which he had promised; the happy effects of which are again set forth by images beautiful and poetical in the highest degree, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.8-Isa.55.13">Isa 55:8-13</reference>. <div eID="gen28700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28701" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen28701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28702" type="x-p"/> Ho, every one that thirsteth - "Water," says Zimchi, "is a metaphor for the law and wisdom: as the world cannot subsist without water, so it is impossible that it can subsist without wisdom. The law is also compared to wine and milk: to wine because wine rejoiceth the heart, as it is written: 'The statutes of the Lord are right, rejoicing the heart,' <reference osisRef="Psa.19.8">Psa 19:8</reference>. It is compared also to milk, because milk is the subsistence of the child; so are the words of the law the nourishment of his soul who walks in the Divine teaching, and grows up under it." <div eID="gen28702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28703" type="x-p"/> Come, buy wine and milk - In ancient times our forefathers used what is now called the old third person singular, ending in eth, for the imperative mood. We have a fine example of His in the first verses of this chapter. I shall present them as they stand in my old MS. Bible: - Alle gee thirstinge cummeth to wateris: and gee that han not sylver, goth forth and bieth, and etith. Cummeth, bieth without silver, and without eny chaungyng, wyn and mylc. Heerith gee, heering me and etith gode thinge, and deliten schal in fattnesse your soule. Bowith in your eie and cummeth to mee, heerith and liven schal your soule. And I shall smyten with gou, everlastynge covenant, the faithful mercies of David.
entries.c03fcda4ba4600e30fcdfb63816b7c5e4bd9a960: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen28703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28704" type="x-p"/> Wherefore do ye spend - Why should ye be so zealously attached to a doctrine from which your souls derive neither comfort nor nourishment?
entries.58080f49937eecbc7703b7a8c47cfd9a29e1a7fe: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen28704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28705" type="x-p"/> I will make an everlasting covenant - Hebrews אכרתה לכם ברית עולם echrethah lachem berith olam, "I will cut the old or everlasting covenant sacrifice with you." That covenant sacrifice which was pointed out of old from the very beginning; and which is to last to the consummation of ages; viz., the Lamb of God that was slain from the foundation of the world. <div eID="gen28705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28706" type="x-p"/> The sure mercies of David - That is, says Kimchi, "The Messiah," called here David; as it is written, "David my servant shall be a prince over you."
entries.b1b60854165e9b5408c6bb6f4ee0dffce12df03f: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen28706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28707" type="x-p"/> Seek ye the Lord while he may be found - Rab. David Kimchi gives the true sense of this passage: "Seek ye the Lord, because he may be found: call upon him, because he is near. Repent before ye die, for after death there is no conversion of the soul."
entries.2ffec7e345b0cc5f1033c8092ff62d03586805ec: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen28707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28708" type="x-p"/> For as the heavens are higher - I am persuaded that כ caph, the particle of comparison, is lost in this place, from the likeness of the particle כי ki, immediately preceding it. So Houbigant and Secker. And their remark is confirmed by all the ancient Versions, which express it; and by the following passage of <reference osisRef="Psa.103.11">Psa 103:11</reference>, which is almost the same: - הארץ על שמים כגבה כי haarets al shamayim chigboah ki יראיו על חסדו גבר yereaiv al chasdo gabar "For as the heavens are high above the earth, <div eID="gen28708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28709" type="x-p"/> So high is his goodness over them that fear him." <div eID="gen28709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28710" type="x-p"/> Where, by the nature of the sentence, the verb in the second line ought to be the same with that in the first; גבה gabah, not גבר gabar: so Archbishop Secker conjectured; referring however to <reference osisRef="Psa.117.2">Psa 117:2</reference>.
entries.898a88a2167082511c2c8e2ce20d261813b4238c: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen28710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28711" type="x-p"/> The mountains and the hills - These are highly poetical images to express a happy state attended with joy and exultation. <div eID="gen28711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28712" type="x-p"/> Ipsi laetitia voces ad sidera jactant <div eID="gen28712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28713" type="x-p"/> Intonsi montes: ipsae jam carmina rupes, <div eID="gen28713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28714" type="x-p"/> Ipsa sonant arbusta. <div eID="gen28714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28715" type="x-p"/> Virg. Ecl. 5:61. "The mountain tops unshorn, the rocks rejoice; <div eID="gen28715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28716" type="x-p"/> The lowly shrubs partake of human voice." <div eID="gen28716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28717" type="x-p"/> Dryden.
entries.4e7a6aebe4a00bbe16bc98bc9e761a77215a2e5d: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen28717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28718" type="x-p"/> Instead of the thorn "Instead of the thorny bushes" - These likewise (see note on <reference osisRef="Isa.55.12">Isa 55:12</reference>, and on <reference osisRef="Isa.54.11">Isa 54:11</reference> (note)) are general poetical images, expressing a great and happy change for the better. The wilderness turned into a paradise, Lebanon into Carmel: the desert of the Gentiles watered with the heavenly snow and rain, which fail not to have their due effect, and becoming fruitful in piety and righteousness: or, as the Chaldee gives the moral sense of the emblem, "instead of the wicked shall arise the just; and instead of sinners, such as fear to sin." Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.35.1">Isa 35:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.35.2">Isa 35:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.41.19">Isa 41:19</reference>. <div eID="gen28718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28719" type="x-p"/> And instead of - The conjunction ו vau is added, ותחת vetachath, in forty-five MSS. of Kennicott's several of De Rossi's, and five editions; and it is acknowledged by all the ancient Versions. The Masoretes therefore might have safely received it into the text, and not have referred us for it to the margin. But this is no uncommon case with them. Even in our own Version the best reading is very often found in the margin.  <chapter eID="Isa.55"/> <div eID="gen28719" type="x-p"/>

entries.a6276ff512cb32cc5138f583770849d38bad4562: <reference osisRef="Isa.55.1-Isa.55.2">Isa 55:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen13544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13545" type="x-p"/> All things are ready; the guests are invited; and nothing is required of them except to come. <hi type="italic">“Alas, all ye thirsty ones, come ye to the water; and ye that have no silver, come ye, buy, and eat! Yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without payment! Wherefore do ye weigh silver for that which is not bread, and the result of your labour for that which satisfieth not? O hearken ye to me, and eat the good, and let your soul delight itself in fat.”</hi> Hitzig and Knobel understand by water, wine, and milk, the rich material blessings which awaited the exiles on their return to their fatherland, whereas they were now paying tribute and performing service inf Babylon without receiving anything in return. But the prophet was acquainted with something higher than either natural water (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.3">Isa 54:3</reference>, cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.41.17">Isa 41:17</reference>) or natural wine (<reference osisRef="Isa.25.6">Isa 25:6</reference>). He knew of an eating and drinking which reached beyond the mere material enjoyment (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.13">Isa 65:13</reference>); and the expression ה טּוּב, whilst it includes material blessings (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.12">Jer 31:12</reference>), is not exhausted by them (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.7">Isa 63:7</reference>, cf., <reference osisRef="Ps.27.13">Psa 27:13</reference>), just as התענּג in <reference osisRef="Isa.58.14">Isa 58:14</reference> (cf., <reference osisRef="Ps.37.4">Psa 37:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.11">Psa 37:11</reference>) does not denote a feeling or worldly, but of spiritual joy. Water, wine, and milk, as the fact that water is placed first clearly shows, are not the produce of the Holy Land, but figurative representations of spiritual revival, recreation, and nourishment (cf., 1Pe 2:2, “the sincere milk of the word”). The whole appeal is framed accordingly. When Jehovah summons the thirsty ones of His people to come to the water, the summons must have reference to something more than the water to which a shepherd leads his flock. And as buying without money or any other medium of exchange is an idea which neutralizes itself in the sphere of natural objects, wine and ilk are here blessings and gifts of divine grace, which are obtained by grace (χάριτι, <hi type="italic">gratis</hi>), their reception being dependent upon nothing but a sense of need, and a readiness to accept the blessings offered. Again, the use of the verb שׁברוּ, which is confined in other passages to the purchase of cereals, is a sufficient proof that the reference is not to natural objects, but to such objects as could properly be compared to cereals. The bread and other provisions, which Israel obtained in its present state of punishment, are called “not bread,” and “not serving to satisfy,” because that which truly satisfies the soul comes from above, and being of no earthly nature, is to be obtained by those who are the most destitute of earthly supplies. Can any Christian reader fail to recall, when reading the invitation in <reference osisRef="Isa.55.1">Isa 55:1</reference>, the words of the parable in <reference osisRef="Matt.22.4">Mat 22:4</reference>, “All things are now ready?” And does not <reference osisRef="Isa.55.2">Isa 55:2</reference> equally suggest the words of Paul in <reference osisRef="Rom.11.6">Rom 11:6</reference>, “If by grace, then is it no more of works?” Even the exclamation <hi type="italic">hoi</hi> (alas! see <reference osisRef="Isa.18.1">Isa 18:1</reference>), with which the passage commences, expresses deep sorrow on account of the unsatisfied thirst, and the toilsome labour which affords nothing but seeming satisfaction. The way to true satisfaction is indicated in the words, “Hearken unto me:” it is the way of the obedience of faith. In this way alone can the satisfaction of the soul be obtained.
entries.e6522dc4b6412506063d14fd5313d9972fbb930f: <reference osisRef="Isa.55.3-Isa.55.5">Isa 55:3-5</reference> <div eID="gen13545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13546" type="x-p"/> And in this way it is possible to obtain not only the satisfaction of absolute need, but a superabundant enjoyment, and an overflowing fulfilment of the promise. <hi type="italic">“Incline your ear, and come to me: hear, and let your soul revive; and I will make an everlasting covenant with you, the true mercies of David. Behold, I have set him as a witness for nations, a prince and commander of nations. Behold, thou wilt call a mass of people that thou knowest not; and a mass of people that knoweth thee not will hasten to thee, for the sake of Jehovah thy God, and for the Holy One of Israel, that He hath made thee glorious.”</hi> The expression “make a covenant” (<hi type="italic">kârath</hi> <hi type="italic">berı̄th</hi>) is not always applied to a superior in relation to an inferior (compare, on the contrary, Ezr 10:3); but here the double-sided idea implied in <hi type="italic">pactio</hi> is confined to one side alone, in the sense of a spontaneous <hi type="italic">sponsio</hi> having all the force of a covenant (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.8">Isa 61:8</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.18">2Ch 7:18</reference>, where <hi type="italic">kârath</hi> by itself signifies “to promise with the force of a covenant”), and also of the offer of a covenant or anticipated conclusion of a covenant, as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.25">Eze 34:25</reference>, and in the case before us, where “the true mercies of David” are attached to the idea of offering or granting involved in the expression, “I will make an everlasting covenant with you,” as a more precise definition of the object. All that is required on the part of Israel is hearing, and coming, and taking: let it do this, and it will be pervaded by new life; and Jehovah will meet with with an everlasting covenant, viz., the unchangeable mercies of David. Our interpretation of this must be dependent chiefly upon whether <reference osisRef="Isa.55.4">Isa 55:4</reference> is regarded as looking back to the history of David, or looking forward to something future. In the latter case we are either to understand by “David” the second David (according to Hos 3:5; <reference osisRef="Jer.30.9">Jer 30:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.24">Eze 34:24</reference>), so that the allusion is to the mercies granted in the Messiah, and according to <reference osisRef="Isa.9.7">Isa 9:7</reference>, enduring “from henceforth even for ever;” or else David is the son of Jesse, and “the mercies of David” are the mercies bestowed upon him, which are called “the true mercies” as mercies promised and running into the future (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.50">Psa 89:50</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.6.42">2Ch 6:42</reference>), in which case <reference osisRef="Isa.55.4">Isa 55:4</reference> explains what David will become in the person of his antitype the second David. The directly Messianic application of the name “David” is to be objected to, on the ground that the Messiah is never so called without further remark; whilst the following objections may be adduced to the indirectly Messianic interpretation of <reference osisRef="Isa.55.4">Isa 55:4</reference> (David in the Messiah). (1.) The change of the tense in <reference osisRef="Isa.55.4">Isa 55:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.5">Isa 55:5</reference>, which requires that we should assume that <reference osisRef="Isa.55.4">Isa 55:4</reference> points backwards into the past, and <reference osisRef="Isa.55.5">Isa 55:5</reference> forwards into the future.<note placement="foot">F. Philippi observes that הן, which refers to the future in <reference osisRef="Isa.55.5">Isa 55:5</reference> at any rate, must be taken as referring to the same sphere of time as that which immediately precedes. But <hi type="italic">hēn</hi> in Isaiah points sometimes backwards (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.1">Isa 50:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.64.4">Isa 64:4</reference>), sometimes forwards; and where two follow one another, of which the one points backwards and the other forwards, the former is followed by the perfect, the latter by the future (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.1-Isa.50.2">Isa 50:1-2</reference>). But if they both point to the future, the future tense is used in both instances (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.9">Isa 50:9</reference>). A better argument in favour of the prophetic interpretation of <reference osisRef="Isa.55.4">Isa 55:4</reference> might be drawn from the fact that נתתּי הן may mean “I give (set, lay, or make) even now” (e.g., <reference osisRef="Jer.1.9">Jer 1:9</reference>). But what we have said above is sufficient proof that this is not the meaning here (if this were the meaning, we should rather expect נתתּיו הן).</note> (2.) That the choice of the expression in <reference osisRef="Isa.55.4">Isa 55:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.5">Isa 55:5</reference> is designed to represent what Israel has to look for in the future as going beyond what was historically realized in David; for in <reference osisRef="Isa.55.5">Isa 55:5</reference> the mass of the heathen world, which has hitherto stood out of all relation to Israel, answers to the לאמּים.   (3.) That the juxtaposition of the Messiah and Israel would be altogether without parallel in these prophecies (chapters 40-66), and contrary to their peculiar character; for the earlier stereotype idea of the Messiah is here resolved into the idea of the “servant of Jehovah,” from which it returns again to its primary use, i.e., from the national basis to the individual, by means of the ascending variations through which this expression passes, and thus reaches a more comprehensive, spiritual, and glorified form. The personal “servant of Jehovah” is undoubtedly no other than the “Son of David” of the earlier prophecy; but the premises, from which we arrive at this conclusion in connection with our prophet, are not that the “servant of Jehovah” is of the seed of David and the final personal realization of the promise of a future king, but that he is of the nation of Israel, and the final personal realization of the idea of Israel, both in its inward nature, and in its calling in relation to the whole world of nations. <div eID="gen13546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13547" type="x-p"/> Consequently <reference osisRef="Isa.55.4">Isa 55:4</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.55.5">Isa 55:5</reference> stand to one another in the relation of type and antitype, and the “mercies of David” are called “the true mercies” (Probably with an allusion to <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.16">2Sa 7:16</reference>; cf., <reference osisRef="Ps.89.29-Ps.89.30">Psa 89:29-30</reference>), as being inviolable-mercies which had both been realized in the case of David himself, and would be realized still further, inasmuch as they must endure for an everlasting future, and therefore be further and further fulfilled, until they have reached that lofty height, on the summit of which they will remain unchangeable for ever. It is of David the son of Jesse that Jehovah says in <reference osisRef="Isa.55.4">Isa 55:4</reference>, “I have given him for a witness to peoples, a leader and commander to the peoples.” So far as the sense is concerned, נגיד is as much a construct as מצוּה. In the application to David of the term עד, which never means anything but <hi type="italic">testis</hi>, witness, in these prophecies, we may clearly see the bent of the prophet’s mind towards what is spiritual. David had subdued nations by the force of arms, but his true and loftiest greatness consisted in the fact that he was a witness of the nations - a witness by the victorious power of his word, the conquering might of his Psalms, the attractive force of his typical life.
