What he expresses so frequently in the Psalms as a resolution and a vow, viz., that he will proclaim the name of Jehovah among the nations (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.50">Psa 18:50</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.57.10">Psa 57:10</reference>), he has really fulfilled: he has not only overcome them by bloody warfare, but by the might of his testimony, more especially as “the sweet psalmist of Israel” (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.1">2Sa 23:1</reference>). What David himself was able to say in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.43">Psa 18:43</reference>, “People that I did not know served me,” will be fulfilled to a still wider extent in the experience of Israel. Having been presented with the promised “inviolable mercies of David,” it will effect a spiritual conquest over the heathen world, even over that portion which has hitherto stood in no reciprocal relation to it, and gain possession of it for itself for the sake of Jehovah, whom it has for its God, and to the Holy One of Israel (ל of the object, in relation to which, or at the instigation of which, anything is done), because He hath glorified it (His people: פארך is not a pausal form for פארך, cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.54.6">Isa 54:6</reference>, but for פארך, פארך, hence = פארך, cf., ענך, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.19">Isa 30:19</reference>); so that joining themselves to Israel is the same as joining themselves to God and to the church of the God of revelation (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.60.9">Isa 60:9</reference>, where <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.55.5">Isa 55:5</reference></hi> is repeated almost word for word).
entries.31f53b120517a2d9c2819a0b926bfa8e727bbc47: <reference osisRef="Isa.55.6-Isa.55.7">Isa 55:6-7</reference> <div eID="gen13547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13548" type="x-p"/> So gracious is the offer which Jehovah now makes to His people, so great are the promises that He makes to it, viz., the regal glory of David, and the government of the world by virtue of the religion of Jehovah. Hence the exhortation is addressed to it in <reference osisRef="Isa.55.6">Isa 55:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.55.7">Isa 55:7</reference> : <hi type="italic">“Seek ye Jehovah while He may be found, call ye upon Him while He is near. Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts: and let him return to Jehovah, and He will have compassion upon him; and to our God, for He will abundantly pardon.”</hi> They are to seek to press into the fellowship of Jehovah (<hi type="italic">dârash</hi> with the radical meaning <hi type="italic">terere</hi>, to acquire experimental knowledge or confidential acquaintance with anything) now that He is to be found (<reference osisRef="Isa.65.1">Isa 65:1</reference>, compare the parallelism of words and things in <reference osisRef="Jer.29.14">Jer 29:14</reference>), and to call upon Him, viz., for a share in that superabundant grace, ow that He is near, i.e., now that He approaches Israel, and offers it. In the admonition to repentance introduced in <reference osisRef="Isa.55.7">Isa 55:7</reference>, both sides of the μετάνοια find expression, viz., turning away from sinful self-will, and turning to the God of salvation. The apodosis with its promises commences with וירחמהוּ - then will He have compassion upon such a man; and consequently לסלוח כּי־ירבּה (with כּי because the fragmentary sentence ואל־אלהינוּ did not admit of the continuation with ו) has not a general, but an individual meaning (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.130.4">Psa 130:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.130.7">Psa 130:7</reference>), and is to be translated as a future (for the expression, compare <reference osisRef="Isa.26.17">Isa 26:17</reference>).
entries.07f7679bdca98044d3f6b4a8f92292c19077a004: <reference osisRef="Isa.55.8-Isa.55.9">Isa 55:8-9</reference> <div eID="gen13548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13549" type="x-p"/> The appeal, to leave their own way and their own thoughts, and yield themselves to God the Redeemer, and to His word, is now urged on the ground of the heaven-wide difference between the ways and thoughts of this God and the despairing thoughts of men (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.27">Isa 40:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.24">Isa 49:24</reference>), and their aimless labyrinthine ways. <hi type="italic">“For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith Jehovah: no, heaven is high above the earth; so high are my ways above your ways, and my thoughts above your thoughts.”</hi> The <hi type="italic">kı̄</hi> (<hi type="italic">imo</hi>) introduces the undeniable statement of a fact patent to the senses, for the purpose of clearly setting forth, by way of comparison, the relation in which the ways and thoughts of God stand to those of man. There is no necessity to supply כאשׁר after כּי, as Hitzig and Knobel do. It is simply omitted, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.62.5">Isa 62:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.3.20">Jer 3:20</reference>, or like כּן in <reference osisRef="Prov.26.11">Pro 26:11</reference>, etc. On what side the heaven-wide elevation is to be seen, is shown in what follows. They are not so fickle, so unreliable, or so powerless.
entries.6692fdaae0a92284bed2554649fadc3f5d3fb63c: <reference osisRef="Isa.55.10-Isa.55.11">Isa 55:10-11</reference> <div eID="gen13549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13550" type="x-p"/> This is set forth under a figure drawn from the rain and the snow. <hi type="italic">“For as the rain cometh down, and the snow from heaven, and returneth not thither, till it has moistened the earth, and fertilized it, and made it green, and offered seed to the sower and bread to the eater; so will my word be which goeth forth out of my mouth: it will not return to me fruitless, till it has accomplished that which I willed, and prosperously carried out that for which I sent it.”</hi> The rain and snow come down from the sky, and return not thither till they have .... The perfects after אם כּי are all to be understood as such (Ewald, §356,<hi type="italic">a</hi>). Rain and snow return as vapour to the sky, but not without having first of all accomplished the purpose of their descent. And so with the word of Jehovah, which goeth forth out of His mouth (יצא, not יצא, <reference osisRef="Isa.45.23">Isa 45:23</reference>, because it is thought of as still going on in the preaching of the prophet): it will not return without having effected its object, i.e., without having accomplished what was Jehovah’s counsel, or “good pleasure” - without having attained the end for which it was sent by Jehovah (constr. as in <reference osisRef="2Sam.11.22">2Sa 11:22</reference>; 1Ki 14:6). The word is represented in other places as the messenger of God (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.8">Isa 9:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.107.20">Psa 107:20</reference>; Psa 147:15.). The personification presupposes that it is not a mere sound or letter. As it goeth forth out of the mouth of God it acquires shape, and in this shape is hidden a divine life, because of its divine origin; and so it runs, with life from God, endowed with divine power, supplied with divine commissions, like a swift messenger through nature and the world of man, there to melt the ice, as it were, and here to heal and to save; and does not return from its course till it has given effect to the will of the sender. This return of the word to God also presupposes its divine nature. The will of God, which becomes concrete and audible in the word, is the utterance of His nature, and is resolved into that nature again as soon as it is fulfilled. The figures chosen are rich in analogies. As snow and rain are the mediating causes of growth, and therefore the enjoyment of what is reaped; so is the soil of the human heart softened, refreshed, and rendered productive or prolific by the word out of the mouth of Jehovah; and this word furnishes the prophet, who resembles the sower, with the seed which he scatters, and brings with it bread which feeds the souls: for every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God is bread (<reference osisRef="Deut.8.3">Deu 8:3</reference>).
entries.7cbf6c3895e91064cc47c5947f163f0f40d915ff: <reference osisRef="Isa.55.12-Isa.55.13">Isa 55:12-13</reference> <div eID="gen13550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13551" type="x-p"/> The true point of comparison, however, is the energy with which the word is realized. Assuredly and irresistibly will the word of redemption be fulfilled. <hi type="italic">“For ye will go out with joy, and be led forth in peace: the mountains and the hills will break out before you into shouting, and all the trees of the field will clap their hands. Instead of the thorn will cypresses shoot up, and instead of the fleabane will myrtles shoot up: and it will be to Jehovah for a name, for an everlasting memorial that will not be swept away.”</hi> “With joy,” i.e., without the hurry of fear (<reference osisRef="Isa.52.12">Isa 52:12</reference>); “in peace,” i.e., without having to fight their way through or flee. The idea of the sufferer falls back in הוּבל behind that of a festal procession (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.15-Ps.45.16">Psa 45:15-16</reference>). In applying the term <hi type="italic">kaph</hi> (hand) to the trees, the prophet had in his mind their <hi type="italic">kippōth</hi>, or branches. The psalmist in <reference osisRef="Ps.98.8">Psa 98:8</reference> transfers the figure created by our prophet to the waves of the streams. <hi type="italic">Na‛ătsūts</hi> (from <hi type="italic">nâ‛ats</hi>, to sting) is probably no particular kind of thorn, such, for example, as the fuller’s thistle, but, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.7.19">Isa 7:19</reference>, briers and thorns generally. On <hi type="italic">sirpad</hi>, see Ges. <hi type="italic">Thes</hi>.; we have followed the rendering, κόυζα, of the lxx. That this transformation of the vegetation of the desert is not to be taken literally, any more than in <reference osisRef="Isa.41.17-Isa.41.20">Isa 41:17-20</reference>, is evident from the shouting of the mountains, and the clapping of hands on the part of the trees. On the other hand, however, the prophet says something more than that Israel will return home with such feelings of joy as will cause everything to appear transformed. Such promises as those which we find here and in <reference osisRef="Isa.41.19">Isa 41:19</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.35.1-Isa.35.2">Isa 35:1-2</reference>, and such exhortations as those which we find in <reference osisRef="Isa.44.23">Isa 44:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.13">Isa 49:13</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Isa.52.9">Isa 52:9</reference>, arise from the consciousness, which was common to both prophets and apostles, that the whole creation will one day share in the liberty and glory of the children of God (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.21">Rom 8:21</reference>). This thought is dressed up sometimes in one for, and sometimes in another. The psalmists after the captivity borrowed the colours in which they painted it from our prophet (see at <reference osisRef="Ps.96.1-Ps.96.13">Psa 96:1-13</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.98.1-Ps.98.9">Psa 98:1-9</reference>). והיה is construed as a neuter (cf., בּראתיו, <reference osisRef="Isa.45.8">Isa 45:8</reference>), referring to this festal transformation of the outer world on the festive return of the redeemed. אות is treated in the attributive clause as a masculine, as if it came from אוּת, to make an incision, to crimp, as we have already indicated; but the Arabic <hi type="italic">âyat</hi>, shows that it comes from אוה, to point out, and is contracted from <hi type="italic">ăwăyat</hi>, and therefore was originally a feminine.  <chapter eID="Isa.55"/> <div eID="gen13551" type="x-p"/>
